newsitem.title: USA: Scrap merchants fret over China waste import rule.
newsitem.headline: Scrap merchants fret over China waste import rule.

text.p: U.S. copper scrap exporters said a new environmental regulation governing waste imports introduced this month by China is becoming a hurdle to trade with one of the world's key red metal markets.

Estelle Wrisley, traffic manager at merchant Alpert & Alpert Iron & Metal in California, said, "This process puts such a gridlock on doing business that it makes it nearly impossible to trade with China."
Bob Stein, manager non-ferrous metals division of Louis Padnos Iron & Metal in Michigan, added, "People are going to get hurt on it."

Robert Wang, manager of China Commodity Inspection Co in Los Angeles, said the Chinese government's China Commodity Inspection Bureau introduced its new rule Nov 1, requiring all imported waste material to be inspected when it is being loaded into a container before it is sealed for shipping to China.
"It you are loading the container at the yard, the inspection should be there," Wang said.
CCIC was asked by the CCIB to carry out the inspections. It charges $400 per day in the Los Angeles area.
Wang said other surveillance companies want to carry out such inspections should apply to the CCIB in Beijing.
Some 400,000 tons of copper scrap was exported to China last year, traders said.

Merchants said the Chinese have been provoked into issuing the decree because they received cargoes of what were labelled scrap steel, metal or other commodities such as waste paper, but have turned out to be hazardous or even radioactive waste.
"The desire of the Chinese government to protect themselves against environmental hazards is absolutely understandable," said Rick Schwartz, executive vice president of Calbag Metals Co of Oregon.
"How the Chinese are going about it is not understandable. The confusion, the ambiguity and impracticality of how they are doing it is very inappropriate," Schwartz added.

Stein said the full effect of the ruling has yet to be felt because many cargoes of U.S. copper exports are shipped through Hong Kong, and China was not in the market to a great extent at present because delivery of shipments booked now would clash with Chinese New Year holidays.
Other merchants feared that deals already in the pipeline, may be affected by the new ruling when the material arrived in China.

Some interpretations of the new ruling or of discussions with several Chinese officials have also indicated that the Chinese henceforth want the scrap to be loose in containers rather than packed as it the traditional form.
